name: The Harmon brothers' household
head: harmon_charles_l

arrival.note: Their father arrived in May 1830 and Andreas says 'his family following him the succeeding year'. The sons are part of that family on the ordinary reading, which puts them in Chicago in 1831; the source does not name them in that sentence.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not attested. The doctor's family that followed him in 1831 comprised a wife and up to nine children, four of whom died in infancy, and no source counts who travelled.

origin.note: Their father practised at Burlington from 1806, married there in 1808, was postmaster there from 1816 and left for the West after reverses in 1829. That is the family's home and the sons' presumed origin; it is not stated of them.

reason_for_coming.value: Following their father west after his business reverses
reason_for_coming.note: 'In 1829 the Doctor suffered some pecuniary reverses and resolved to attempt recuperation in the Great West.' The sons' own motive is not recorded.

works_at.note: A DISCREPANCY CARRIED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED, and it is already on the building record: Andreas names the concern 'Harmon's and Loomis's' while the 1833 advertisement is headed 'C. & I. HARMON' and names no Loomis. Those are compatible - and note that Loomis is the brothers' own middle name and their mother's maiden name, Welthyan Loomis - but they are not the same statement.

present_on_scene_date.note: Documented trading in November 1833; nothing follows the firm to 1835. Their father left for Texas in 1834 and they did not.

FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Chas. L. Harmon” (f1839_v0709, printed page 40, ward 1). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 6 times, as “HARMON CHARLES L”, “HARMON CHAS L”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-30: 1 federal land entry — NW sec 04 T39N R13E and 4 lots in the platted town — lot 10 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L10BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 7 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L7BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 8 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L8BL20CHIV, as printed); lot 9 of block 20 in the town the register codes CHIV (L9BL20CHIV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — BL137 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 80.45 acres stated in all, for $5540.55 (ls0227, ls1210, ls1211, ls1212, ls1213, ls0751). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $5310.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. merge_ruling.for_merge: 'Isaac' is identical and the surnames differ by one interior vowel. Isaac Dewey Harmon is documented and anchored — Fergus's old-settler notice of 9 April 1886, the 1833 tax list, the Black Hawk muster of 1832, the Democrat of 17 December 1833 and 5 August 1835 — and the `harmon-isaac` cluster has already folded a bare 'Isaac Harmon' onto him under C3 as the one Isaac Harmon the town documents. An 'Isaac Harman' on the 1834 poll looks like the same man with the vowel mis-set.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE ROLL THAT SETS HARMAN SETS HARMON ON THE NEXT TWO LINES, FOR OTHER MEN. The poll filed 11 August 1834 enters 'Harman, Isaac' at voter_lists_1833_1835.txt line 219 and then 'Harmon, C. L.' at 220 and 'Harmon, M. D.' at 221 — one roll, one clerk, both spellings, deliberately distinguished within three lines. That is the opposite of C9's demonstration: the printing is caught keeping the spellings apart. Isaac Dewey Harmon's own readings are on the 1833 tax list and not on that poll, so no roll sets both spellings for HIM; and the Harmon stem is heavily populated here — harmon_charles_l, harmon_d, harmon_elijah_d, harmon_isaac_d, harmon_m_d, five cards — while Harman has one. D9, and the C3 fold inside the `harmon-isaac` cluster is untouched because it folded a card spelled Harmon.

research_note: TWO BROTHERS IDENTIFIED BY CROSS-READING TWO CHAPTERS OF THE SAME BOOK, which is the kind of result this layer exists to produce: a newspaper masthead of initials becomes two named men with a father, a home town and a reason for being in Illinois. THE THIRD HARMON IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. An Isaac Harmon was the town's clerk and collector in 1833-34 and is not written here, because Andreas's 1832 militia list carries two distinct Isaac Harmons and this project cannot tell which is which. That is a documented resident consciously left out of the count rather than guessed into it.

Names, places * , dates, and ages at death
of some of Chicago's Old Settlers, prior to 1843, and other well - known citizens who arrived after 1843, together
with others prominently connected with Illinois history:
old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.
